title: Getting medical care as a student
summary: A short guide to registering with a GP, using NHS services and knowing where to find official healthcare information as a student.
whyItMatters: International students may be unfamiliar with how UK healthcare access works.
keyPoints: Registering with a GP near university can make it easier to access care when needed.
NHS 111 can help when you need medical help now but it is not life-threatening.
Always use official NHS or university guidance for current healthcare information.
sourceNote: HealthLens-created summary based on official NHS and UKCISA sources. Check linked original sources for the latest information.

title: Vitamin D in the UK winter
summary: A short guide to official UK information about vitamin D, autumn and winter sunlight, and where to read NHS guidance.
whyItMatters: Students arriving from sunnier countries may not expect how limited UK winter sunlight can affect vitamin D guidance.
keyPoints: NHS guidance says people in the UK should consider taking a daily vitamin D supplement during autumn and winter.
This guide does not provide personal medical advice or dosage advice.
Students should read NHS guidance or speak to a healthcare professional if unsure.
sourceNote: HealthLens-created summary based on official NHS and GOV.UK sources. Does not provide personal medical advice.

title: Pharmacy, GP, NHS 111 or 999?
summary: A service-navigation guide explaining common UK healthcare routes without assessing symptoms.
whyItMatters: Students new to the UK may not know the difference between pharmacy advice, GP appointments, NHS 111 and emergency services.
keyPoints: Pharmacies can advise on common minor illnesses and medicines questions.
NHS 111 is for medical help now when it is not life-threatening.
Call 999 or go to A&E for life-threatening emergencies or serious injuries.
sourceNote: HealthLens-created service navigation summary. Does not assess symptoms or recommend treatment.

title: Managing stress during assessment periods
summary: A short guide to recognising assessment pressure, using support early and finding trusted wellbeing resources.
whyItMatters: Academic pressure can affect sleep, motivation and confidence, especially for students adjusting to a new education system.
keyPoints: Asking for help early is usually better than waiting until problems escalate.
University wellbeing services and student support teams can help students understand available options.
Urgent mental health concerns should use official urgent support routes.
sourceNote: HealthLens-created summary based on university and NHS wellbeing signposting. Does not provide medical advice.

title: Understanding tenancy deposits
summary: A short guide to deposit protection, common renting concerns and where to find expert housing advice.
whyItMatters: International students may be unfamiliar with UK renting rules and may not know where to get advice.
keyPoints: Deposits and tenancy responsibilities should be checked through expert housing advice.
Students should keep written records of agreements, payments and repair requests.
This guide signposts to housing advice and does not provide legal advice.
sourceNote: HealthLens-created summary based on Shelter, Citizens Advice and Bristol SU housing signposting. Does not provide legal advice.

title: Budgeting for university life
summary: A guide to planning everyday costs, recurring bills and safer spending habits as a student in the UK.
whyItMatters: International students often need to adapt to a new cost-of-living environment, banking system and spending pattern.
keyPoints: Budgeting should include rent, bills, food, transport, course costs and social spending.
Student discounts can help, but they should not replace a basic budget.
This guide signposts to money guidance and does not provide financial advice.
sourceNote: HealthLens-created summary based on MoneyHelper and UCAS signposting. Does not provide financial advice.

title: Student discounts without overspending
summary: A short guide to using student discounts carefully without turning savings into unnecessary spending.
whyItMatters: Discount platforms can be useful, but they can also encourage purchases students did not originally need.
keyPoints: Check whether a discount reduces an expense you already planned.
Compare total cost, not only percentage discount.
Avoid treating discount platforms as financial advice.
sourceNote: HealthLens-created summary referencing student money guidance and Save the Student. Commercial platforms are not financial advice or product recommendations.

title: First month in the UK checklist
summary: A practical checklist for the first month in the UK, including healthcare, banking, support services and everyday setup.
whyItMatters: New international students often need to complete several practical tasks before they feel settled.
keyPoints: Register with a GP and learn how NHS services work.
Set up essential practical services such as banking, SIM card and university support access.
Use UKCISA and university guidance for current international student information.
sourceNote: HealthLens-created checklist based on UKCISA and university signposting. Check linked original sources for current guidance.
